Yeah, that saved my design. I knew nothing about ASICs. Luckily Luke taught me about reset. Pure luck. I really don’t want any shorts.

boards arrived! hope they work 😅

Oh in the future I'd probably not skip the back side coverlay over the die.
And I'd probably prefer to keep the backside ground plane over the die just not over the pads like that; and in the future don't align the hatching lines or other lines orthogonal to the major bending; i.e., try to keep copper lines from being parallel to the cylinder axis around which the board will be bent. 

In this case, it'd better be 45° rotated from now.
Even if they're aligned with the bond wire's axis?

Alignment with the bond wire has no correlation to anything with setup. Landing locations are just chosen more or less arbitrarily. When the landing locations are linear it seemed like it was easier for them to edit when problems came up, as they could sortof bulk edit. When all the landings were along some arc there was nothing to reference as they're all independent. 
I hope I'm explaining that right
Ohhhh

I'd assume then a 2/3 row staggered landing pad geometry with otherwise nice axis aligned grid spacing would not be substantially worse to program and would get much more density than the current single row non-staggered one?

Like, the pads on the PCB are much coarser than PCB DRC minimums for copper width/spacing, and those are again coarser than the die side bond pad minimum spacing, and IIRC wedge bonds are a symmetric tool action to attach the wire to the substrate? 
Just that to end the wire it gets ripped off kinda horizontally in the same direction it came from after attaching to the surface; while ball bonding is very different between start and end action?
Basically the tool's UI has a thing where you can say I'm placing 10 bonds in a row and then you mark the first and last bond and it places them evenly spaced between them.
ohhhhh. good/fair
The whole configuration is manual and entered via a keyboard on a computer.
I'm still very interested in potentially purchasing a wire bonding machine and retrofitting the control system with a RPi that can do all this stuff automatically without having any human do setup.
It could then collect photos of the bonds as they are done as well.
hmmmm, yeah, I'm surprised it's done all so manually still today, not even loaded from a floppy levels of pre-programming....
and presumably bespoke bonding configurations as long as they can get checked by some reasonable DRC gate that keeps the machine from choking /hitting anything in the porcess?

messages.content: So I'm noodling around http://blog.reprap.org (yes, http) working on an Open Source 3D printed 3D printer that can not only replicate like the original RepRap, but also shrink itself. It's called RepRapMicron. So far we're down to 4um features and repeatable 3-axis positioning to better than a micron. It's all 3D printed, hardware store parts, or from the CNC/3D printer world (use whatever controller you like). Now, Diffraction Limited used a UV fibre source to cure resin, and got a lot of views. RepRapMicron deliberately didn't go down that path because it doesn't scale, but seeing as people seem to like it, here's RepRapMicron doing a 250um wide "Hello, World" anyway. It's remarkably flexible, and made from Nail Art UV resin.
Should you want to build one the madness begins here https://github.com/VikOlliver/RepRapMicron/wiki

messages.content: It looks like I see an optical fiber

On Tuesday I gave a little open-silicon back-end tutorial, using LibreLane and the wafer.space template to build a tiny cryptography ASIC, to mostly total beginners at the Practical Open Silicon Workshop (POpSi) https://popsi-workshop.org in Bochum, Germany. Room was full and the tutorial was well received I believe (despite me being a bit disorganized) 😁 Here's the material, in case anyone wants to do similar things in the future: https://github.com/ThorbenMoos/FOSSi_Tutorial. Slides also feature some wafer.space stuff and community contributions.
